title: Recursion, DP and Greedy Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on recursion, memoization vs tabulation, the classic DP patterns (knapsack, LIS, LCS, grid paths, coin change), when greedy works and fails, and backtracking basics.

chapters.title: Recursion and the DP Mental Model
points: Recursion = base case + recursive case that shrinks the problem; a missing or unreachable base case gives stack overflow
Each call gets its own stack frame; depth n costs O(n) space (Python's default limit is ~1000 frames)
Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure are the two conditions that make DP applicable
Naive fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) is O(2^n) because the same subproblems are recomputed; DP cuts it to O(n)
DP recipe: define the state, write the recurrence, set base cases, fix the evaluation order, then read off the answer

chapters.title: Memoization vs Tabulation
points: Memoization is top-down: recursion plus a cache keyed by state (dict or @lru_cache), computing only the states actually reached
Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table iteratively from the base cases, so there is no recursion and no stack-depth risk
Both give the same time complexity: number of states × work per transition
Rolling arrays cut space: fib needs two variables, and a 2D table that reads only the previous row needs one row
Choose memo when few states are reachable or the order is awkward; choose tabulation for deep recursion or when space optimization matters
Gotcha: a mutable argument (list) cannot be a cache key, so convert it to a tuple or an index

chapters.title: Knapsack, Coin Change and Grid Paths
points: 0/1 knapsack: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val[i] + dp[i-1][w-wt[i]]); O(nW) time, and a 1D version iterates w downward so an item is not reused
Unbounded knapsack and coin change iterate w upward because items may repeat
Coin change minimum coins: dp[a] = min(dp[a-c] + 1) with dp[0]=0 and dp initialised to infinity; unreachable stays infinity, so return -1
Counting ways with coins: loop coins in the outer loop and amounts in the inner loop to count combinations; swap the loops and you count permutations
Grid paths: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1] with the first row and column set to 1 up to the first obstacle and 0 from it onward, and obstacle cells set to 0; O(mn) time, one row of space

chapters.title: LIS and LCS
points: LCS state dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j of b; O(mn)
LCS recurrence: if a[i]==b[j] then dp[i-1][j-1]+1, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
Subsequence is not substring: a subsequence keeps order but may skip characters, and a substring must be contiguous
LIS O(n^2): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j<i with a[j]<a[i]; the answer is max(dp), not dp[n-1]
LIS O(n log n): keep a tails array and use bisect_left for a strictly increasing result (bisect_right for non-decreasing); the array length is the answer but is not itself a valid LIS

chapters.title: Greedy and Backtracking
points: Greedy takes the locally best choice and never revisits it; it is correct only with the greedy-choice property, usually proven by an exchange argument
Greedy works: interval scheduling (sort by end time), fractional knapsack (sort by value/weight), Huffman coding
Greedy fails: coin change with coins {1,3,4} for amount 6 gives 4+1+1 = 3 coins, while the optimum is 3+3 = 2 coins, and 0/1 knapsack needs DP
Backtracking template: choose, recurse, un-choose, with a copy of the path saved at the leaf; use it for subsets, permutations and N-Queens
Prune early by checking constraints before recursing; sort and skip equal neighbours (if i>start and a[i]==a[i-1]: continue) to avoid duplicate results
Complexity: subsets O(2^n), permutations O(n!); backtracking is exponential, so use DP instead if subproblems overlap

chapters.title: DP and Greedy Cheat Sheet
points: Pattern pick: choose or skip means knapsack; compare two sequences means LCS; best ending at i means LIS; reach a target with repeats means coin change; move right or down means grid
Loop direction: 0/1 knapsack 1D goes w downward, unbounded goes upward
Complexity table: fib memo O(n); knapsack O(nW); LCS O(mn); LIS O(n log n); coin change O(amount × coins)
Decision order: try greedy and look for a counterexample, then DP if subproblems overlap, then backtracking if you need all solutions
Interview Point: Is it memoization or tabulation, and what is the state? Why does greedy fail on coins {1,3,4}? How do you avoid duplicate subsets in backtracking?
